### II.1 Vortex Geometry

Consider attaching a vortex at a generic point ${\boldsymbol{r}}_{0}$ :

$$ \psi\mapsto\tilde{\psi}=(\mathsf{z}({\boldsymbol{r}})-\mathsf{z}({\boldsymbol{r}}_{0}))\psi. $$

We call this “vortex attachment” because $\tilde{\psi}$ has a zero at ${\boldsymbol{r}}_{0}$ and winds by a $\pm 2\pi$ phase around it. This creates a dip in probability density near the position ${\boldsymbol{r}}_{0}$ where the wavefunction vanishes; at the many body level these will become “correlation holes”. Near the point ${\boldsymbol{r}}_{0}$ we have

$$ \lvert\tilde{\psi}({\boldsymbol{r}}-{\boldsymbol{r}}_{0})\rvert^{2}=g_{\mu\nu}({\boldsymbol{r}}_{0})r^{\mu}r^{\nu}\,\lvert\psi({\boldsymbol{r}}_{0})\rvert^{2}+O({\boldsymbol{r}}^{3}), $$

where $g_{\mu\nu}({\boldsymbol{r}})=\Re\partial_{\mu}\overline{\mathsf{z}}({\boldsymbol{r}})\partial_{\nu}\mathsf{z}({\boldsymbol{r}})$ is a “vortex metric” that describes the elliptical shape of the vortex core, such that the semimajor and semiminor lengths $\lambda_{1,2}(\boldsymbol{r}_{0})$ are the eigenvalues of $g(\boldsymbol{r}_{0})$ . We note the overall scale of $\mathsf{z}$ and $g$ is not fixed.

To eliminate pathological cases, we impose a non-degeneracy condition. A function $\mathsf{z}:\mathbb{R}^{2}\to\mathbb{C}$ is a vortex function if the vortex-metric eigenvalues are uniformly bounded above and below:

$$ c^{-1}\leq\lambda_{1,2}(\boldsymbol{r})\leq c. $$

This ensures the vortex cores do not get arbitrarily large, small, or squeezed. In fact, (5) implies the vortex function $\mathsf{z}:\mathbb{R}^{2}\to\mathbb{C}$ is invertible, such that there exists coordinates ${\boldsymbol{r}}^{\prime}({\boldsymbol{r}})=(x^{\prime},y^{\prime})$ where $\mathsf{z}=x^{\prime}+iy^{\prime}$ , through a global version of the inverse function theorem, see Ref. 72.

We caution that the diffeomorphism $\boldsymbol{r}\mapsto{\boldsymbol{r}}^{\prime}$ does not mean that any vortexable band is physically equivalent to one with $\mathsf{z}=x+iy$ . This is because distances are not preserved under the diffeomorphism so, e.g., Coulomb interactions $V(r)=1/\lVert{\boldsymbol{r}}\rVert\neq 1/\lVert{\boldsymbol{r}}^{\prime}\rVert$ single out the “laboratory” frame, which we use unless otherwise stated. However, the ${\boldsymbol{r}}^{\prime}$ coordinates will give a convenient link to momentum space band geometry.

The vortex metric is part of a Hermitian metric:

$$ \displaystyle\eta_{\mu\nu}({\boldsymbol{r}}) \displaystyle=\partial_{\mu}\overline{\mathsf{z}({\boldsymbol{r}})}\partial_{\nu}\mathsf{z}({\boldsymbol{r}}), \displaystyle g_{\mu\nu}({\boldsymbol{r}})=\Re\eta_{\mu\nu}({\boldsymbol{r}}), \displaystyle\Omega({\boldsymbol{r}})\varepsilon_{\mu\nu}=\Im\eta_{\mu\nu}({\boldsymbol{r}}). $$

We call $\Omega$ the vortex chirality because the phase winding of vortices is $\operatorname{sign}(\Omega)2\pi$ , which reverses under $\mathsf{z}\leftrightarrow\overline{\mathsf{z}}$ . The non-singular metric $g$ implies that $\Omega$ does not vanish or change sign, such that the vortex phase winding is the same everywhere, because the rank one nature of $\eta$ implies $\det g=\lvert\Omega\rvert^{2}$ . In fact, vortex chirality is tied to Chern number: $\Omega C\geq 0$ : we show this in the first section of the supplementary material (SI). We note in passing that the condition $\det g=\lvert\Omega\rvert^{2}$ specifies a real-space Kähler structure, reminiscent of that of MSBG [31].

### II.2 Uniqueness

Can a vortexable band have two or more distinct vortex functions? With relatively weak assumptions we can show that this is not the case. In the SI we show that the vortex function is unique up to affine transformations $\mathsf{z}\to\alpha\mathsf{z}+\beta$ if the following conditions hold (Prop 3:

- 1. The vortexable band has a discrete translation symmetry with translation operator $\mathcal{T}_{\boldsymbol{a}}$ , in the sense that $[\mathcal{T}_{\boldsymbol{a}},\mathcal{P}]=0$ and $\partial_{\mu}\mathsf{z}({\boldsymbol{r}}+{\boldsymbol{a}})=\partial_{\mu}\mathsf{z}({\boldsymbol{r}})$

- 2. The electron density at full filling, $\rho(\boldsymbol{r})=\sum_{\alpha}\left|\psi_{\alpha}({\boldsymbol{r}})\right|^{2}$ , is finite, continuous, and almost always nonzero.

Let us briefly comment on the two conditions. We view the discrete translation symmetry condition as a technical tool but not a strong physical restriction. Indeed, we make no assumption on how large the unit cell is or how many Bloch bands are encompassed by the vortexable “band”, and we expect most condensed matter systems to be translation symmetric in the limit of thermodynamically large unit cells. A condition on the density $\rho({\boldsymbol{r}})$ is necessary to eliminate pathological density profiles: it is always possible to modify the vortex function on regions of vanishing electron density.

## III Vortexable bands admit pseudopotential FQH Trial States

We now construct FQHE ground states from vortexable bands, and demonstrate they are exact many-body ground states for short range (pseudopotential) interactions (SRI-GS). At the single particle level, iterating (2) implies 22 2 Note that $f(\mathsf{z})$ is not a “new” vortex function, since $f$ must be linear else the non-degeneracy condition is not satisfied. Indeed, $f^{\prime}(\mathsf{z})$ is either constant or unbounded by Liouville’s theorem, and the metric associated to $f(\mathsf{z})$ is $\lvert f^{\prime}(\mathsf{z})\rvert^{2}\partial_{\mu}\overline{\mathsf{z}}\partial_{\nu}\mathsf{z}+\text{c.c.}$ .

$$ f(\mathsf{z})\psi=\mathcal{P}f(\mathsf{z})\psi\text{ for holomorphic }f(\mathsf{z})=\sum_{n\geq 0}f_{n}\mathsf{z}^{n}. $$

Next, at the many-body level, we may apply (7) to each particle of the system to obtain

$$ f(\mathsf{z}_{1},\ldots,\mathsf{z}_{N})\ket{\Psi}=\mathscr{P}f(\mathsf{z}_{1},\ldots,\mathsf{z}_{N})\ket{\Psi}, $$

where $\mathscr{P}=\otimes_{i}\mathcal{P}_{i}$ is the many body projector, $\mathsf{z}_{i}=\mathsf{z}({\boldsymbol{r}}_{i})$ is the vortex operator for particle $i$ , $f$ is holomorphic in each $\mathsf{z}_{i}$ , and $\ket{\Psi}=\mathscr{P}\ket{\Psi}$ is any initial state of electrons in the band of interest. The ability to attach holomorphic functions to many body wavefunctions in vortexable bands generalizes any trial wavefunction in the LLL to any vortexable band. We focus on Laughlin-like states

$$ \ket{\Psi^{(2s)}_{\mathsf{z}}}=\prod_{i<j}(\mathsf{z}_{i}-\mathsf{z}_{j})^{2s}\ket{\Psi}, $$

so we may make pseudopotential arguments, but we imagine future works will find interest in examining composite Fermi liquids or Pfaffian states in vortexable bands. We additionally emphasize that while we are inspired by the Laughlin construction, the construction (9) applies to any vortexable band, and can lead to states qualitatively different than Laughlin states (for example, in vortexable bands with higher Chern number).

As two particles $i$ and $j$ approach each other at a center-of-mass position ${\boldsymbol{r}}_{0}$ , the probability density associated to (9) vanishes as

$$ \lvert\Psi^{(2s)}_{\mathsf{z}}\rvert^{2}\propto\lvert g_{\mu\nu}({\boldsymbol{r}}_{0})r_{-}^{\mu}r_{-}^{\nu}\rvert^{4s}, $$

where ${\boldsymbol{r}}_{-}={\boldsymbol{r}}_{i}-{\boldsymbol{r}}_{j}$ is the relative coordinate. The high power $4s$ by which (9) vanishes ensures that $\ket{\Psi^{(2s)}_{\mathsf{z}}}$ is a SRGS[51]; see the supplementary material for a pedagogical review of this argument. Note that we focus on a density-drensity interaction Hamiltonian — the vortexable band should have zero bare dispersion. As we will see in the examples section, this is typically automatic.

The reader may worry that vortex attachment would also generate FCI ground states in a topologically trivial band ( $C=0$ ). In the first section of the SI we show that $C=0$ vortexable bands instead admit a basis of delta-function-localized position eigenstates (similar to a single band tight binding model or a free particle). The ability to ultra-localize electrons in a band projected manner implies that it is straightforward to keep them apart. Indeed, for $C=0$ vortexable bands a simple charge density wave is a zero-energy ground state of any potential with range strictly less than the interparticle spacing.

We have argued that topological vortexable bands with zero dispersion host FCI ground states in the limit of short range interactions. However, this limit may be hard to reach if the Berry curvature is highly inhomogeneous. Indeed, consider the extreme limit of a soleinoidal Berry curvature. For a finite size system with periodic boundary conditions, such that momentum space is discretized, the Berry curvature is completely invisible to the momentum space grid. In this case the band can energetically resemble a trivial band, see e.g. Ref. [73].

## IV Chiral models as an origin of vortexability

We have shown that vortexable bands generalize the LLL in such a way to preserve vortex attachment and the ensuing energetic arguments for hosting SRI-GS. However, vortexable bands can and do arise in systems quite dissimilar to free electrons in a magnetic field. We now consider four examples of vortexable bands: two have $\mathsf{z}\neq x+iy$ , two have no magnetic field, and one has arbitrary Chern number $C>1$ .

Our examples have a common origin: a continuum chirally symmetric model $\{H,\sigma_{z}\}=0$ . These models have the general form

$$ H=\begin{pmatrix}0&D^{\dagger}\\
D&0\end{pmatrix},\qquad\sigma_{z}=\begin{pmatrix}I&0\\
0&-I\end{pmatrix}, $$

for some operator $D$ . If $D$ satisfies both of the following two conditions then the space of zero modes of $D$ is a vortexable band.

- P1. $[D,\mathsf{z}({\boldsymbol{r}})]=0$ for a vortex function $\mathsf{z}$ .

- P2. $D$ has an extensive number of zero modes.

Property P1 holds when the dependence of $D$ on derivatives $\partial_{x}$ and $\partial_{y}$ is through a single differential operator with complex valued-coefficients $\overline{\partial_{\mathsf{z}}}$ . Solving the Beltrami equation $\overline{\partial_{\mathsf{z}}}\mathsf{z}=0$ then yields a vortex function that satisfies $[D,\mathsf{z}]=0$ .

### E1: Strained Graphene in Magnetic Field (Nonlinear $\mathsf{z}(\boldsymbol{r})$ ).

Our first example demonstrates that nonlinear vortex functions $\mathsf{z}({\boldsymbol{r}})$ arise naturally in strained graphene. When placed on a bumpy surface, or subject to external stress, the atoms of a graphene lattice are displaced by $\boldsymbol{u}(\boldsymbol{r})$ which modifies the lab-frame metric of the graphene surface. Indeed, the graphene sheet is an embedded surface with (lab frame) metric $g_{\mu\nu}(\boldsymbol{r})=\delta_{\mu\nu}+2u_{\mu\nu}(\boldsymbol{r})=\delta_{ab}e_{\mu}^{a}({\boldsymbol{r}})e_{\nu}^{b}({\boldsymbol{r}})$ where $u_{\mu\nu}=[\partial_{\mu}u_{\nu}+\partial_{\nu}u_{\mu}]/2$ is the strain tensor and $e^{a}_{\mu}(\boldsymbol{r})=\delta^{a}_{\mu}+\delta^{a\nu}u_{\mu\nu}$ . Here $\delta$ is always the Kronecker delta regardless of index positions. We will use shortly use the inverse metric $g^{\mu\nu}$ to raise indices: $e^{\mu}_{a}=g^{\mu\nu}e_{\nu}^{a}$ . The latin index positions do not matter (they are raised and lowered by $\delta^{ab}$ ).

The uneven distances between atomic sites modifies the velocity operator to $\hat{v}^{\mu}=ve^{\mu}_{a}({\boldsymbol{r}})\sigma^{a}$ , whose anisotropy and position dependence is encoded into the orthonormal basis $e^{\mu}_{a}({\boldsymbol{r}})$ . The continuum Hamiltonian is then [74, 75, 76, 77, 78, 79, 80, 81, 82, 83, 84].

$$ H_{\text{strained graphene}}(\boldsymbol{r})=ve^{\mu}_{a}({\boldsymbol{r}})\sigma^{a}(-i\partial_{\mu}-A^{\rm{eff}}_{\mu}), $$

where $A^{\rm{eff}}_{\mu}=\mathcal{A}^{\rm el}_{\mu}(\boldsymbol{r})+A^{\rm ext}_{\mu}(\boldsymbol{r})$ . Here $A^{\rm ext}_{\mu}(\boldsymbol{r})$ is the magnetic vector potential and $\mathcal{A}^{\rm el}_{\mu}(\boldsymbol{r})$ is a pseudomagnetic vector potential due to the elastic modulation of the hopping matrix elements $t(a_{0})\mapsto t(a_{0}+u(\boldsymbol{r}))$ . Note that there are also other terms that are second order in gradients that arise from the hopping modulation [80, 82, 85, 86]; we ignore them here for simplicity though they do not change our conclusions which will be based on topology and the Dirac nature of (12).

When written in the form (11), the zero mode operator $D$ of (12) is

$$ D_{\text{strained graphene}}=2v\chi^{\mu}({\boldsymbol{r}})(-i\partial_{\mu}-A_{\mu}^{\rm{eff}}), $$

where $\chi^{\mu}=\frac{1}{2}(e^{\mu}_{1}+ie_{2}^{\mu})$ . The vortex operator is now obtained by solving the Beltrami equation

$$ \chi^{\mu}({\boldsymbol{r}})\partial_{\mu}\mathsf{z}=\overline{\partial_{\mathsf{z}}}\mathsf{z}=0, $$

such that property P1 is satisfied.

The easiest way to achieve P2 is a magnetic field $B_{0}\hat{z}=\nabla\times A^{\rm{ext}}$ , but experiments have also found strain Landau levels with $\mathcal{A}^{\rm{el}}\neq 0$ , $A^{\rm{ext}}=0$ [87]. In either case, the number of zero modes is tied to the number of flux quanta by an index theorem [40] (see e.g. [88] Eq. 12.86).

$$ \text{dim}\ker D-\text{dim}\ker D^{\dagger}=N_{\phi}=\int{\boldsymbol{\nabla}}\times{\boldsymbol{A}}^{\rm eff}d^{2}{\boldsymbol{r}}, $$

such that the number of zero modes $\text{dim}\ker D$ is bounded below by $N_{\phi}$ , which is typically extensive in the system size. Therefore Eq. (12) gives an experimentally-realizable vortexable band without any translation symmetry and vortex $\mathsf{z}\neq x+iy$ . Indeed, $\mathsf{z}(\boldsymbol{r})$ is typically nonlinear in $\boldsymbol{r}$ .

### E2: Chiral Twisted Bilayer Graphene (no magnetic field)

We will now show how chiral twisted bilayer graphene yields a vortexable band with no magnetic field. Ordinary twisted bilayer graphene (TBG) contains tunneling matrix elements for inter-sublattice tunneling and intra-sublattice tunneling. However the energetic preference for local AB over AA stacking induces lattice deformations [89, 84, 90, 91], leading to a suppression of the AA tunneling, as well as an experimentally-unavoidable internal strain field that we will discuss later. The suppression of the AA tunneling motivated Ref. [38] to consider an idealized limit of zero AA tunneling. The Hamiltonian is then of the form (11) with

$$ D_{\rm{TBG}}=\begin{bmatrix}-2iv\overline{\partial}&w_{1}U_{1}(\boldsymbol{r})\\
w_{1}U_{1}(-\boldsymbol{r})&-2iv\overline{\partial}.\end{bmatrix}, $$

where $U_{1}(\boldsymbol{r})=\sum_{n=0}^{2}e^{in\phi-i\boldsymbol{q}_{n}\cdot\boldsymbol{r}}$ , $\boldsymbol{q}_{n}=C_{3z}^{n}k_{\theta}(0,-1)$ , $\phi=\tfrac{2\pi}{3}$ , $k_{\theta}=|\boldsymbol{K}^{\rm{top}}-\boldsymbol{K}^{\rm{bot}}|$ , and $w_{1}\approx$110\text{\,}\mathrm{m}\mathrm{e}\mathrm{V}$$ is the AB interlayer tunnelling. Note that $D_{\text{TBG}}$ only depends on the antiholomorphic derivative $\overline{\partial}=\frac{1}{2}(\partial_{x}+i\partial_{y})$ . The spectrum of the Hamiltonian defined with (16) depends only on the dimensionless parameter $\alpha=w_{1}/v_{F}k_{\theta}$ , up to an overall scale $v_{F}k_{\theta}$ .

The operator (16) satisfies P1 for $z=x+iy$ and, at the ‘magic angle’ $\alpha\approx 0.586$ , P2 is satisfied as well. Here $D_{\mathrm{TBG}}$ has an extensive number of zero modes [38, 47] that form a $C=1$ band, despite the lack of an external magnetic field. Indeed, the origin of P2 is not the index theorem (15), as $\dim\ker D=\dim\ker D^{\dagger}$ for all $\alpha$ . We conclude that there are examples of vortexable bands with no external magnetic field.

The same relaxation mechanisms that led to suppressed $AA$ tunneling yields equal and opposite strain in both layers: $\boldsymbol{u}_{+}=-\boldsymbol{u}_{-}$ [84, 89]. The resulting pseudomagnetic field $\mathcal{B}(\boldsymbol{r})=\nabla\times\mathcal{A}(\boldsymbol{r})$ is moiré periodic, equal and opposite in the layers, and averages to zero over each moiré unit cell, but has peaks of ${\sim}80$ $\mathrm{T}$ [84, 89].

It is interesting to examine the effect of this heterostrain on the vortexability of (16). We will see that while P2 is satisfied at a renormalized angle, P1 no longer holds. With strain effects taken into account, we obtain

$$ D_{\rm{TBG}}^{(\alpha_{s})}=\begin{bmatrix}2v\chi_{+}^{\mu}(-i\partial_{\mu}+\alpha_{s}\mathcal{A}_{\mu})&w_{1}U_{1}(\boldsymbol{r})\\
w_{1}U_{1}(-\boldsymbol{r})&2v\chi_{-}^{\mu}(-i\partial_{\mu}-\alpha_{s}\mathcal{A}_{\mu})\end{bmatrix}, $$

Property P2 remains satisfied. Indeed, Refs [92, 45, 46] show the existence of a magic angle is robust to symmetry-preserving perturbations, which is indeed the case for realistic $\mathcal{A}(\boldsymbol{r})$ [84]. Furthermore, the position-dependent Fermi velocities, which lead to $\chi_{\pm}\neq\frac{1}{2}\begin{pmatrix}1&i\end{pmatrix}$ , do not change the band energies. Indeed, we may work in the crystal frame of unperturbed atomic positions where $\chi^{\mu}\partial_{\mu}\to\overline{\partial}$ . Thus, we still obtain an exactly flat band at a suitably renormalized $\theta(\alpha_{s})$ . We show in Fig. 2 how the magic angle changes with $\alpha_{s}\mathcal{A}(\boldsymbol{r})$ , $0\leq\alpha_{s}\leq 1$ , giving rise to a “magic line” of bands without any external magnetic field.

However, the different complex differential operators $\chi_{\pm}^{\mu}({\boldsymbol{r}})\partial_{\mu}$ , associated with the opposite strains in both layers prevent us from defining a single vortex function $\mathsf{z}$ that commutes with (17) in the lab frame. Thus, property P1 is not satisfied. It is possible to define a generalized “layer dependent vortex operator” $\tilde{\mathsf{z}}=\diag(\mathsf{z}_{+},\mathsf{z}_{-})$ that satisfies $[D,\tilde{\mathsf{z}}]=0$ and $\tilde{\mathsf{z}}\psi=\mathcal{P}\tilde{\mathsf{z}}\psi$ . But $\tilde{\mathsf{z}}$ does not lead to a SRI-GS because on-site inter-layer repulsion is no longer screened: $\mathsf{z}_{+}({\boldsymbol{r}})-\mathsf{z}_{-}({\boldsymbol{r}})\neq 0$ .

We note that (17) was recently studied in the final section of Ref. [86], where a flat band also appeared. In their chiral model, the authors of [86] work consistently to a lower order in gradients and hence do not include the position-dependent Fermi velocity, such that their chiral Hamiltonian may be interpreted as the crystal frame version of (17). With this approximation, (17) is vortexable with $z=x+iy$ (and therefore hosts SRI-GS). Note that previous non-chiral Hamiltonains in Refs. [86, 85] do include the position dependent Fermi velocity as well as other non-geometrical effects at the same order in gradients. Amongst the second order in gradient terms, we have kept only the geometric position-dependent Fermi velocity in order to study its effect on vortexability from a conceptual point of view.

### E3: Degenerate Landau Levels in Chirally stacked Graphene (Multiple bands, total $C>1$ ).

For the next two examples we will focus on vortexable bands with higher Chern number. For simplicity, we will consider unstrained graphene and obtain standard vortex functions $z=x+iy$ ; strain may be included straightforwardly but here we want to emphasize the emergence of higher Chern numbers.

Recall that by “band” we mean “low energy subspace with an extensive number of states”; vortexable bands can consist of multiple Bloch bands or Landau levels. In Bernal bilayer graphene it is well known that the zeroth and first Landau level are degenerate at zero energy [93, 94]. This pattern extends to chirally-stacked graphene multilayers[95, 96, 97] where Landau levels $0$ through $n-1$ are degenerate, where $n$ is the number of layers[98]. To understand the vortexability of the combined set of Landau levels, consider the Hamiltonian for AB stacked Bernal bilayer graphene in a constant magnetic field $B_{0}$ :

$$ H_{\text{Bernal-Bilayer}}=\begin{pmatrix}0&D^{\dagger}_{1}&0&0\\
D_{1}&0&\gamma&0\\
0&0&0&D^{{\dagger}}_{1}\\
0&0&D_{1}&0\end{pmatrix}. $$

In (18) the Hamiltonian acts on a wavefunction $\begin{pmatrix}\psi_{A1}&\psi_{B1}&\psi_{A2}&\psi_{B2}\end{pmatrix}^{T}$ . The interlayer tunneling strength is $\gamma$ , and

$$ D_{1}=2v(-i\overline{\partial}_{z}-\overline{A}_{z})=\sqrt{2}v\ell^{-1}\hat{a} $$

is the monolayer zero mode operator where $\overline{\partial}_{z}=\frac{1}{2}(\partial_{x}+i\partial_{y})$ , $\overline{A}_{z}=\frac{1}{2}(A_{x}+iA_{y})$ , $\hat{a}$ is the standard Landau level lowering operator, and $\ell=1/\sqrt{B}$ is the magnetic length. We have neglected smaller interlayer hoppings [99].

Let us write (18) in the form (11). We obtain

$$ D_{\text{Bernal-Bilayer}}=\begin{pmatrix}D_{1}&\gamma\\
0&D_{1}\end{pmatrix}. $$

There are two types of zero modes of (20) corresponding to a zeroth and first Landau level

$$ \psi_{0}=\begin{pmatrix}\psi_{\text{LLL}}\\
0\end{pmatrix}\qquad\psi_{1}=\begin{pmatrix}\hat{a}^{\dagger}\psi_{\text{LLL}}\\
-\frac{\sqrt{2}v}{\ell\gamma}\psi_{\text{LLL}}\end{pmatrix}. $$

Here $\psi_{\text{LLL}}$ is a LLL state which satisfies $\hat{a}\psi_{\text{LLL}}=\hat{a}z\psi_{\text{LLL}}=0$ . The combined zero mode subspace (21), consisting of the zeroth and first Landau level together, is a vortexable band: the zero mode operator (20) commutes with $z$ . The space spanned by the zeroth Landau level $\psi_{0}$ is also vortexable on its own. However, the first Landau level on its own is not vortexable. Indeed, direct calculution shows that $z\psi_{1}$ has spectral weight in the zeroth Landau level, i.e. states of the form $\psi_{0}$ (21), because $[a^{\dagger},z]\neq 0$ .

We may similarly write down the zero mode operator for $n$ -layer chiral graphene which has the inductive form

$$ D_{n}=\begin{pmatrix}D_{1}&\boldsymbol{\gamma}_{n-1}\\
0&D_{n-1}.\end{pmatrix} $$

where $\boldsymbol{\gamma}=(\gamma,0,\ldots,0)$ is an $(n-1)$ -dimensional hopping vector which we take to be nearest-neighbor for simplicity. The lowest $n$ Landau levels are therefore vortexable zero mode subspace of (22), with total Chern number $C=n$ .

### E4: Chiral Graphene multilayers ( $C>1$ , no magnetic field)

Our final example constructs vortexable bands with arbitrary Chern number $C>1$ without an external magnetic field. Our construction uses twisted chiral graphene multilayers [48, 100, 101]: these are the structures above except the bottom layer is replaced by a chiral twisted bilayer graphene system. While this example is nominally that of a single physical system, we expect the general structure of this example to be a source of future zero-field higher Chern vortexable bands.

Our zero mode operator is given by

$$ D_{n}=\begin{pmatrix}-2iv\overline{\partial}_{z}&\boldsymbol{\gamma}_{n}\\
0&D_{n-1}\end{pmatrix}. $$

with $D_{1}=D_{\textrm{TBG}}$ such that $D_{n}$ is associated with a chiral TBG system at its magic angle with $n-1$ monolayers stacked on top with zero twist angle such that each pair of monolayers is AB-stacked Bernal graphene.

The zero mode Bloch-periodic wavefunctions $\psi^{(n)}_{{\boldsymbol{k}},\ell}({\boldsymbol{r}})$ of $D_{n}$ on layer $1\leq\ell\leq n$ may be obtained as

$$ 2iv\overline{\partial}\psi^{(n)}_{{\boldsymbol{k}},1}({\boldsymbol{r}})=\gamma\psi^{(n)}_{{\boldsymbol{k}},2}({\boldsymbol{r}}),\quad\psi^{(n)}_{{\boldsymbol{k}},\ell}=\lambda_{\boldsymbol{k}}\psi^{(n-1)}_{{\boldsymbol{k}},\ell+1}, $$

where $\lambda_{\boldsymbol{k}}$ is ${\boldsymbol{k}}$ -dependent but otherwise constant.

The first equation of (24) is generically solvable through Fourier series $\psi^{(n)}_{{\boldsymbol{k}},\ell<n}({\boldsymbol{r}})=e^{i{\boldsymbol{k}}\cdot{\boldsymbol{r}}}\sum_{\boldsymbol{G}}u^{(n)}_{{\boldsymbol{k}}\ell<n}({\boldsymbol{G}})e^{i{\boldsymbol{G}}\cdot{\boldsymbol{r}}}$ where ${\boldsymbol{k}}$ is measured from the K point (for the $n$ ’th layer the periodicity is different due to the twist angle, though this will not play a role here [48]). However, there is a single value ${\boldsymbol{k}}=0$ in the first Brillouin Zone for which there is an obstruction to inverting Eq. (24). Indeed, we obtain

$$ -iv(k+G)u^{(n)}_{{\boldsymbol{k}},1}({\boldsymbol{G}})=\gamma u^{(n)}_{{\boldsymbol{k}},2}({\boldsymbol{G}})=\gamma\lambda_{\boldsymbol{k}}u^{(n-1)}_{{\boldsymbol{k}},1}({\boldsymbol{G}}), $$

where $k=k_{x}+ik_{y}$ and $G=G_{x}+iG_{y}$ . Because $u^{(n-1)}_{{\boldsymbol{k}}=-{\boldsymbol{G}},1}({\boldsymbol{G}})\neq 0$ generically, which we have verified numerically for this system, we must have $\lambda_{{\boldsymbol{k}}=-{\boldsymbol{G}}}=0$ for all reciprocal lattice vectors ${\boldsymbol{G}}$ . The additional phase winding associated with this zero leads to an increase in Chern number $C_{n}=C_{n-1}+1$ ; see Ref. [48] for details. Since the zero mode operator satisfies $[D_{n},z]=0$ , we conclude that we have found a class of vortexable Bloch bands with arbitrary Chern number.

## V Connection to momentum space band geometry

We now specialize to the case of lattice translations, whereupon vortexability will become a computable & quantifiable notion, and an organizing principle for many ideas in band geometry. “Trace condition” bands are always special vortexable bands, with a linear vortex function $\mathsf{z}=x+iy$ . We show the converse fails; the “trace condition” is insufficient to identify general vortexable bands where $\mathsf{z}(\boldsymbol{r})$ is nonlinear, such as E1 and E2 above. We then identify the point of failure — the choice $u_{\boldsymbol{k}}(\boldsymbol{r})=e^{-i\boldsymbol{k}\cdot\boldsymbol{r}}\psi_{\boldsymbol{k}}(\boldsymbol{r})$ in Bloch’s theorem. We end with a general formula, Eq. (39), that detects if a band is vortexable or nearly vortexable. Throughout the section we assume that the vortexable bands of interest satisfy the mild conditions in Sec. II.2.

### V.1 Traditional Band Geometry and Vortexability with $x+iy$

We first recall some standard definitions and results on band geometry. Consider a Chern $C$ band with an orthonormal basis $\ket{\psi_{\boldsymbol{k}a}}$ . Throughout this section we set $C,\Omega(\boldsymbol{r})\geq 0$ (the other case follows from complex conjugation). Momentum space band geometry characterizes the gauge-invariant part of the Bloch periodic wavefunctions $\ket{u_{\boldsymbol{k}a}}:=e^{-i\boldsymbol{k}\cdot\boldsymbol{r}}\ket{\psi_{\boldsymbol{k}a}}$ through the Berry curvature $\mathcal{F}(\boldsymbol{k})$ and Fubini-Study metric $g_{\mathrm{FS}}(\boldsymbol{k})$ [102]. These are defined by (see e.g. [7, 27, 103])

$$ g_{\mathrm{FS}}^{\mu\nu}({\boldsymbol{k}})=\Re\tilde{\eta}^{\mu\nu}({\boldsymbol{k}}),\quad\mathcal{F}({\boldsymbol{k}})\varepsilon^{\mu\nu}=-\frac{1}{2}\Im\tilde{\eta}^{\mu\nu}({\boldsymbol{k}}), $$

where

$$ \tilde{\eta}^{\mu\nu}(\boldsymbol{k})=\sum_{a}\braket{\partial^{k_{\nu}}u_{\boldsymbol{k}a}|Q_{\boldsymbol{k}}|\partial^{k_{\mu}}u_{\boldsymbol{k}a}} $$

is the positive semidefinite quantum geometric tensor and $Q_{\boldsymbol{k}}=I-\sum_{a}\ket{u_{\boldsymbol{k}a}}\bra{u_{\boldsymbol{k}a}}$ . The lowest Landau level is entirely specified by its band geometry: any $C=1$ band where (I) the trace inequality

$$ \int\tr g_{\mathrm{FS}}(\boldsymbol{k})\;d^{2}\boldsymbol{k}\geq 2\pi C $$

is saturated [the trace condition] and (II) $\mathcal{F}(\boldsymbol{k})$ is constant — is equivalent to the LLL [37]. The idea of “Landau level mimicry” is that, so long as (I) and (II) are nearly satisfied then, by adiabatic continuity, the band is likely to host a FCI phase. We reiterate that vortexable bands go beyond mimicry, hosting FQHE states in bands that do not resemble the LLL, with e.g. inhomogeneous Berry curvature or higher Chern number. Furthermore, in the SI (Sec. D) we use our beyond-mimicry perspective to analyze other previously proposed band-geometric conditions such as the “determinant condition”, which we argue to be generically unrelated to the physics of the FQHE (Sec. D.3).

With this choice, and after a suitable non-unitary gauge transformation, the Bloch wavefunctions $u^{\prime}$ can be chosen to be holomorphic in $k_{x}+ik_{y}$ . Topologically nontrivial vortexable bands lead to SRI-GS: FQHE ground states in the limit of short range interactions.*

Bands satisfy the trace condition if and only if they are vortexable with $\mathsf{z}({\boldsymbol{r}})=x+iy$ . Note that vortexibility involves multiplication of the $\psi$ wavefunctions by a position operator whereas band geometry consists of differentiating the $u$ wavefunctions with respect to ${\boldsymbol{k}}$ . These settings are bridged by the product rule (as in Fourier transforms) through the definition $\ket{u_{\boldsymbol{k}a}}:=e^{-i\boldsymbol{k}\cdot\boldsymbol{r}}\ket{\psi_{\boldsymbol{k}a}}$ :

$$ -i{\boldsymbol{\nabla}}_{\boldsymbol{k}}\ket{\psi_{\boldsymbol{k}}^{a}}=\hat{{\boldsymbol{r}}}\ket{\psi_{\boldsymbol{k}}^{a}}+e^{i{\boldsymbol{k}}{\boldsymbol{r}}}(-i{\boldsymbol{\nabla}}_{\boldsymbol{k}})\ket{u_{\boldsymbol{k}}^{a}}. $$

Acting with $\mathcal{Q}:=1-\mathcal{P}=1-\sum_{{\boldsymbol{k}}a}\ket{\psi_{{\boldsymbol{k}}a}}\bra{\psi_{{\boldsymbol{k}}a}}$ annihilates the left hand side of Eq. (29), which can be seen by writing the $k$ derivative as a finite difference between wave-functions at two nearby $k$ points, and realizing that each of them belongs to the band and is hence annihilated by $\mathcal{Q}$ . This gives:

$$ \mathcal{Q}{\boldsymbol{r}}\ket{\psi_{\boldsymbol{k}}^{a}}=\mathcal{Q}ie^{i{\boldsymbol{k}}\cdot{\boldsymbol{r}}}{\boldsymbol{\nabla}}_{\boldsymbol{k}}\ket{u_{\boldsymbol{k}}^{a}}. $$

For clarity, the projector $\mathcal{Q}$ acts on Bloch periodic wavefunctions $\ket{\psi_{\boldsymbol{k}}}$ and contains a sum over ${\boldsymbol{k}}$ , whereas $Q({\boldsymbol{k}})$ acts on periodic wavefunctions, appears in the definition of quantum geometry (27), and contains no sum over ${\boldsymbol{k}}$ . Since $\bra{\psi_{{\boldsymbol{k}}^{\prime}}}e^{i{\boldsymbol{k}}\cdot{\boldsymbol{r}}}\nabla_{\boldsymbol{k}}\ket{u_{\boldsymbol{k}}}$ vanishes for ${\boldsymbol{k}}\neq{\boldsymbol{k}}^{\prime}$ by translation symmetry, we have $\mathcal{Q}e^{i{\boldsymbol{k}}\cdot{\boldsymbol{r}}}{\boldsymbol{\nabla}}_{\boldsymbol{k}}\ket{u_{{\boldsymbol{k}}}}=e^{i{\boldsymbol{k}}\cdot{\boldsymbol{r}}}Q({\boldsymbol{k}}){\boldsymbol{\nabla}}_{\boldsymbol{k}}\ket{u_{{\boldsymbol{k}}}}$ , a rewriting of the right hand side of (30). Multiplication by $\boldsymbol{\omega}^{(0)}=\begin{pmatrix}1&i\end{pmatrix}^{T}$ then yields

$$ \mathcal{Q}z\ket{\psi_{{\boldsymbol{k}}a}}=0\iff Q({\boldsymbol{k}})\overline{\partial}_{k}\ket{u_{{\boldsymbol{k}}a}}=0, $$

where $z=x+iy$ and $2\overline{\partial}_{k}=\partial_{k_{x}}+i\partial_{k_{y}}$ . The right hand side of (31) vanishes for all ${\boldsymbol{k}},a$ if and only if the trace condition is satisfied:

$$ \displaystyle\int d^{2}{\boldsymbol{k}}(\tr g_{\mathrm{FS}}({\boldsymbol{k}})-\mathcal{F}({\boldsymbol{k}})) \displaystyle=\int d^{2}{\boldsymbol{k}}\;\omega_{\mu}^{(0)}\tilde{\eta}^{\mu\nu}({\boldsymbol{k}})\overline{\omega}_{\mu}^{(0)} \displaystyle=\sum_{a}\int d^{2}{\boldsymbol{k}}\;\lVert Q({\boldsymbol{k}})\overline{\partial}_{k}u_{\boldsymbol{k}}^{a}\rVert^{2}. $$

Thus a band is vortexable with $\mathsf{z}=x+iy$ if and only if the trace condition is satisfied, and deviations can quantified using $\int\tr g_{\mathrm{FS}}d^{2}{\boldsymbol{k}}-2\pi C\geq 0$ .

A powerful alternative way to think about the trace condition is through $k$ -space holomorphicity. The trace condition holds if, and only if, the Bloch wavefunctions $u_{\boldsymbol{k}}$ can be written as holomorphic functions of $k=k_{x}+ik_{y}$ after a non-unitary gauge transformation $\tilde{u}_{\mathsf{k}}=S_{\boldsymbol{k}}u_{\boldsymbol{k}}$ [31]. Here $S_{\boldsymbol{k}}$ is an invertible matrix at each $\boldsymbol{k}$ , and acts by matrix multiplication in band indices. This claim is proven in the SI (see Prop 2 and Sec. D.2). The key point is that the right-hand side of Eq. (31) is a gauge-invariant version of the Cauchy-Riemann equations. If $Q({\boldsymbol{k}})\overline{\partial}_{k}\ket{u_{{\boldsymbol{k}}a}}=0$ , one may always solve $P({\boldsymbol{k}})\overline{\partial}_{k}(S_{\boldsymbol{k}}\ket{u_{\boldsymbol{k}}})=0$ to fix a $k$ -holomorphic gauge. Brillouin zone holomorphicity provides exceptionally strong constraints on the single-particle wavefunctions of vortexable bands, and is a key tool in our uniqueness result Prop. 3.

The structures we have described in this subsection is a special case, corresponding to $\mathsf{z}=x+iy$ , of the interrelations depicted in Fig. 3. We will now cover the general case, with arbitrary $\mathsf{z}$ and a suitably modified trace condition.

### V.2 Bloch’s Theorem and General Vortexability

General vortexable bands are vortexable bands where $\mathsf{z}(\boldsymbol{r})$ is a nonlinear function of $\boldsymbol{r}$ . In light of examples E1 and E2 this class is physically relevant, leading to a natural question: given a band, how can one compute if it is a generally vortexable band? We must go beyond the trace condition Eq. (28) which is equivalent to vortexability with $z=x+iy$ . Traditional band geometry (26) can only detect linear vortex functions (special vortexability). The limitation is the single ${\boldsymbol{k}}$ -derivative acting on $\ket{u_{\boldsymbol{k}}}$ in (26), which translates to a single power of the position operator ${\boldsymbol{r}}$ through the differentiation of $u_{\boldsymbol{k}}({\boldsymbol{r}})=e^{-i{\boldsymbol{k}}\cdot{\boldsymbol{r}}}\psi_{\boldsymbol{k}}({\boldsymbol{r}})$ [see e.g. (29)]. Thus we can only have an equivalence (31) for linear vortex functions for this definition of $\ket{u_{{\boldsymbol{k}}a}}$ .

However, we can instead define

$$ \ket{u^{\prime}_{{\boldsymbol{k}}a}}=e^{-i{\boldsymbol{k}}\cdot{\boldsymbol{r}}^{\prime}}\ket{\psi_{{\boldsymbol{k}}a}} $$

where ${\boldsymbol{r}}^{\prime}({\boldsymbol{r}}+{\boldsymbol{a}})={\boldsymbol{r}}^{\prime}({\boldsymbol{r}})+{\boldsymbol{a}}$ . This, in turn, defines $\mathcal{F}^{\prime}$ and $g_{FS}^{\prime}$ . The reasoning above (31) then yields

$$ \mathcal{Q}z^{\prime}\ket{\psi_{{\boldsymbol{k}}a}}=0\iff Q({\boldsymbol{k}})\overline{\partial}_{k}\ket{u^{\prime}_{{\boldsymbol{k}}a}}=0, $$

such that the trace condition (28), defined using the wavefunctions $\ket{u^{\prime}_{{\boldsymbol{k}}a}}$ is equivalent to vortexability with $\mathsf{z}=z^{\prime}=x^{\prime}+iy^{\prime}$ . We underscore that (33) is not related to the usual definition by a gauge transformation. Indeed, such a transformation is akin to changing unit cell embedding in tight-binding models and yields different values for gauge-invariant quantities such as the Berry curvature: $\mathcal{F}_{\boldsymbol{k}}^{\prime}\neq\mathcal{F}_{\boldsymbol{k}}$ [103]. We note that the traditional choice $\ket{u_{{\boldsymbol{k}}a}}=e^{-i{\boldsymbol{k}}\cdot{\boldsymbol{r}}}\ket{\psi_{{\boldsymbol{k}}a}}$ is often convenient; for example electric fields couple via $\boldsymbol{E}\cdot\boldsymbol{r}$ such that the traditional $\ket{u_{\boldsymbol{k}}}$ appears in semiclassical transport [103]. For our purposes, however, widening our scope to the modification (33) is essential.

We now show how (33) and (34) characterize general vortexable bands, starting with the case of rotational symmetry for simplicity. Any vortex function may be written as $\mathsf{z}({\boldsymbol{r}})=x^{(\mathsf{z})}+iy^{(\mathsf{z})}$ where ${\boldsymbol{r}}^{\mathsf{z}}({\boldsymbol{r}}):\mathbb{R}^{2}\to\mathbb{R}^{2}$ is a diffeomorphism [see below Eq. (5)]. With $n>2$ -fold rotation symmetry, vortex functions obey $\mathsf{z}({\boldsymbol{r}}+{\boldsymbol{a}})=\mathsf{z}({\boldsymbol{r}})+a_{x}+ia_{y}$ under translations (see SI Prop. 4). Then ${\boldsymbol{r}}^{(\mathsf{z})}({\boldsymbol{r}}+{\boldsymbol{a}})={\boldsymbol{r}}^{(\mathsf{z})}({\boldsymbol{r}})+{\boldsymbol{a}}$ such that the wavefunctions $\ket{u^{(\mathsf{z})}_{{\boldsymbol{k}}a}}=e^{-i{\boldsymbol{k}}\cdot{\boldsymbol{r}}^{(\mathsf{z})}}\ket{\psi_{{\boldsymbol{k}}a}}$ are periodic and (34) is satisfied for $\mathsf{z}=x^{(\mathsf{z})}+iy^{(\mathsf{z})}$ . We define

$$ T=\left[\min_{{\boldsymbol{r}}^{\prime}({\boldsymbol{r}})}\int\tr g^{\prime}_{\mathrm{FS}}\;d^{2}{\boldsymbol{k}}\right]-2\pi C\geq 0 $$

where $\boldsymbol{r}^{\prime}$ runs over lattice-periodic, orientation-preserving diffeomorphisms. A ( $C_{n\geq 2}$ symmetric) band is vortexable (with $C,\Omega(\boldsymbol{r})\geq 0$ ) if and only if $T=0$ . The minimizing diffeomorphism $\boldsymbol{r}^{\prime}=(x^{\prime},y^{\prime})$ gives the vortex function $\mathsf{z}=x^{\prime}+iy^{\prime}$ .

The modification (35) of band geometry was previously proposed in Ref. [103] in the tight-binding setting (see also [104] for $C=0$ ). There it was interpreted as a choice of unit cell embedding in tight binding models. Here it emerges naturally for continuum vortexable bands in terms of the choice of periodic wavefunction (33): this is precisely where the choice of coordinate frame or unit cell embedding enters band geometry.

For bands without rotational symmetry, we must modify Eq. (35) slightly. In general (see SI Props 1 & 2),

$$ \mathsf{z}(\boldsymbol{r}+\boldsymbol{a})=\mathsf{z}(\boldsymbol{r})+\omega_{\mu}a^{\mu}, $$

for some complex vector $\boldsymbol{\omega}=\boldsymbol{\omega}^{(0)}J$ where $\boldsymbol{\omega}^{(0)}=\begin{pmatrix}1&i\end{pmatrix}^{T}$ and $J$ is a $2\times 2$ invertible matrix. Note that the transformation

$$ {\boldsymbol{r}}\to J^{-1}{\boldsymbol{r}},\quad{\boldsymbol{a}}\to J^{-1}{\boldsymbol{a}},\quad{\boldsymbol{k}}\to{\boldsymbol{k}}J, $$

reduces us to the rotationally-symmetric case. Therefore we require a form of the trace condition that is invariant under linear transformations.

The reformulation of the trace condition we need is the zero mode condition $\omega_{\mu}\tilde{\eta}^{\mu\nu}({\boldsymbol{k}})=0$ for $\boldsymbol{k}$ -independent $\omega_{\mu}$ [42]. It is invariant under linear transformations induced by (37), $\boldsymbol{\omega}\to\boldsymbol{\omega}J^{-1}$ and $\tilde{\eta}\to J\eta J^{T}$ , and it reduces to the the usual trace condition $\omega^{(0)}_{\mu}\tilde{\eta}^{\mu\nu}=0$ [see (32)] under a suitable choice of $J$ . Such a zero mode $\omega_{\mu}$ exists if and only if $\det\tilde{\eta}_{I}=0$ with

$$ \tilde{\eta}_{I}=\int_{\text{BZ}}\tilde{\eta}(\boldsymbol{k})\,d^{2}\boldsymbol{k}, $$

because $\tilde{\eta}({\boldsymbol{k}})$ is positive definite for each ${\boldsymbol{k}}$ . Let us then define

$$ T=\min_{{\boldsymbol{r}}^{\prime}({\boldsymbol{r}})}2\sqrt{\det\tilde{\eta}_{I}}\geq 0, $$

such that a band with discrete translation symmetry is vortexable with a translationally symmetric vortex function $\partial_{\mu}\mathsf{z}({\boldsymbol{r}})=\partial_{\mu}\mathsf{z}({\boldsymbol{r}}+{\boldsymbol{a}})$ if and only if $T=0$ in (39). The vortex function is given as $\mathsf{z}=\omega_{\mu}r^{\prime\mu}$ where ${\boldsymbol{r}}^{\prime}({\boldsymbol{r}})$ is the minimizing diffeomorphism of (39) and $\omega_{\mu}$ is the zero mode that leads to the vanishing of $\det\tilde{\eta}_{I}$ . We have included a square root and factor of $2$ such that (39) reduces to (35) in the rotationally symmetric case. It would be interesting to study the regime of “nearly” vortexable bands where $T$ is small but non-zero.

## VI Conclusions

In this work we have introduced vortexable bands: bands which admit vortex attachment through a complex valued function $\mathsf{z}({\boldsymbol{r}})$ . These bands allow construction of SRI-GS— exact many-body FQHE ground states in the limit of short-range interactions. Vortexable bands emerge naturally in graphene-based systems with or without magnetic field, with arbitrary Chern number, and with arbitrary vortex functions $\mathsf{z}({\boldsymbol{r}})$ . A subset of “special” vortexable bands, with $\mathsf{z}=x+iy$ and discrete translation symmetry, may be characterized using traditional approaches to momentum space band geometry, in particular the trace condition. By moving beyond the conventional choice of periodic wavefunctions $u_{\boldsymbol{k}}({\boldsymbol{r}})=e^{-i{\boldsymbol{k}}\cdot{\boldsymbol{r}}}\psi_{\boldsymbol{k}}({\boldsymbol{r}})$ we arrived at a formula that can check if any band is vortexable.

Our treatment of vortexable bands opens up a number of new directions for future investigation. What types of vortexable bands are possible? Can we characterize the single particle wavefunctions? Can we define the real-space geometry of general bands, such that the Kahler geometry (6) emerges when the band is vortexable? How can we understand the interplay between interaction range and Berry curvature inhomogeneity? What types of FCIs do they host, especially with higher Chern number? How do composite Fermi liquids or non-Abelian states behave in generic vortexable bands? What happens to excitations like Skyrmions or magneto-roton modes in vortexable bands that are dissimilar to the LLL? Chern bands with small dispersion and small $T$ [Eq. (35)] should host FCIs — can one derive a quantitative relation to the many-body gap? Are vortexable bands of equal and opposite Chern numbers ideal for other phases such as superconductors? We believe that future work will focus on the above questions and more.

More broadly, vortexable bands combine the analytic tractability of the LLL with much of the diversity of topological bands in condensed matter systems (in particular, magnetic translation symmetry and flat Berry curvature is not required). We therefore argue that vortexability will provide a central conceptual role in the rich and emerging field of interacting topological bands.
